title: Did Romans eat fast food?
hook: Pompeii had about 80 street-food counters, and one of them kept its own menu.
summary: In a way, yes: Pompeii had about 80 thermopolia, counters selling hot food and drinks, and one fully excavated in 2020 kept its paintings and traces of food.
cardText: In a way, yes. Pompeii had about 80 thermopolia, street counters selling hot food and drinks, because eating the midday meal out was common.

cardBlocks.text: Picture a masonry counter facing the street, with big clay jars set into it, where you order a hot dish. That was a thermopolium, a name of Greek origin for places that served hot food and drinks. Across the Roman world, people often ate their midday meal away from home, and Pompeii alone had about 80 of these counters.

In December 2020, archaeologists unveiled a thermopolium excavated in its entirety for the first time. Its counter is painted with two mallard ducks hanging upside down, a rooster and a dog on a lead. The jars held bones of duck, pig, goat, fish and land snails: the paintings showed, at least in part, what was sold there.
Eating out was a Roman habit: Pompeii had about 80 hot-food counters, and one of them preserved its menu.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The thermopolium lies in Regio V, one of the regions Pompeii was divided into in the 19th century. Part of it surfaced in 2019, during work to stabilise the edges of the excavation. The front of the counter shows a Nereid, a sea nymph, riding a sea horse. On the side, a painting probably shows the shop itself, like a trademark. Amphorae, tall clay jars, were found in front of the counter, matching the painting.

At the bottom of a jar used for wine were broken or ground beans. According to the Roman writer Apicius, they were used to change the wine’s taste and colour, making it paler. In a corner lay the skeleton of a very small adult dog, about 20 to 25 centimetres at the shoulder, nothing like the muscular dog in the painting.

There were also bones of at least two people. One was 50 or older and was probably lying on some kind of bed when the pyroclastic flow arrived. On the frame around the painted dog, someone scratched a mocking inscription, perhaps to tease the owner, perhaps the work of someone who worked there.

claims.text: Thermopolia served hot food and drinks, stored in large clay jars set into a masonry counter; the name is of Greek origin.

support.excerpt: Thermopolia were places where, as the name of Greek origin would suggest, drinks and hot foods were served, and these goods were stored in largedolia (jars) which were embedded in the masonry serving counter.

claims.text: In the Roman world, it was common to eat the meal away from home.

support.excerpt: Such establishments were located all over the Roman world, when it was common to go out to eat the prandium (meal).
At Pompeii alone, there are around eighty of them.
Romans in the ancient city of 13,000 near Naples would snack on meals (prandia) outside the home from more than 80 walkup snack shops in Pompeii alone, scientists said.

claims.text: In December 2020, archaeologists unveiled a Pompeii thermopolium excavated in its entirety for the first time.

support.excerpt: Dec. 26 (UPI) -- Pompeii archaeologists on Saturday unveiled the site of a snack shop for hot foods covered with colorful frescoes in the ancient city.
because for the first time an area of this type has been excavated in its entirety

claims.text: The counter is painted with two mallard ducks hanging upside down, a rooster and a dog on a lead.

support.excerpt: Colorful decorations on the counter included a sea nymph riding a seahorse, along with still-life scenes of animals including two mallard ducks hanging upside down, a rooster and a dog on a leash

claims.text: The counter’s jars held bones of duck, pig, goat, fish and land snails.

support.excerpt: The paintings on the counter include two mallard ducks, and indeed a fragment of duck bone was in fact found inside one of the containers, alongside swine, goats, fish and land snails, indicating the great variety of products of animal origin used in the preparation of the dishes.

claims.text: The counter paintings show, at least in part, the food and drink sold there.

support.excerpt: The first analyses confirm that the paintings on the counter depict, at least in part, the foodstuffs and drinks which were actually sold inside the Thermopolium.

claims.text: Part of the thermopolium was uncovered in 2019, during work to stabilise the edges of the excavation.

support.excerpt: The commercial structure had only been partially studied in 2019, during the interventions of the Great Pompeii Project aimed at stabilising and consolidating the historic excavation fronts.

claims.text: The front of the counter shows a Nereid on a sea horse, and the side probably depicts the shop itself, like a trademark.

support.excerpt: The decorations on the counter - which were the first to emerge during the excavation - comprise the image of a Nereid riding a sea-horse in a marine setting on the front, while the shorter side features an illustration which is probably of the shop itself, like a kind of trademark.
Colorful decorations on the counter included a sea nymph riding a seahorse, along with still-life scenes of animals including two mallard ducks hanging upside down, a rooster and a dog on a leash

claims.text: At the bottom of a wine jar were broken or ground beans, which Apicius says were used to change the wine’s taste and colour.

support.excerpt: At the bottom of a dolium - which has been identified as a container for wine on the basis of the bottle for drawing the liquid that was found inside it - the presence of beans was detected, which had been intentionally broken apart or ground. In his De re Coquinaria (I,5), Apicius explains the reason for this, asserting that they were used in order to modify the taste and colour of the wine, bleaching it.

claims.text: The skeleton of a very small adult dog, 20–25 cm at the shoulder, was found in the shop.

support.excerpt: It was not a large and muscular dog like the one depicted on the counter, but an extremely small specimen, about 20-25cm high at the shoulder despite being an adult dog.

claims.text: One victim was at least 50 and was probably on some kind of bed when the pyroclastic flow arrived; there were bones of at least one other person.

support.excerpt: Several belong to an individual of at least fifty years of age, who at the moment when the pyroclastic current arrived, was most likely on some kind of bed
Other bones, which are yet to be investigated, belong to another individual

claims.text: Pompeii is divided into regions (regiones), a system set up by Fiorelli.

support.excerpt: divided it into a system of 'regiones', 'insulae' and 'domus'

claims.text: Amphorae found in front of the counter matched the ones in the painting.

support.excerpt: The discovery of amphorae, which were located in front of the counter, reflected the painted image exactly.

claims.text: A mocking inscription was scratched on the frame of the dog painting, perhaps by a prankster teasing the owner or by someone who worked there.

support.excerpt: A mocking inscription can be found scratched onto the frame which surrounds the painting of the dog
This was probably left by a prankster who sought to poke fun at the owner, or by someone who worked in the Thermopolium.
